newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Hyder yr profits rise, savings eyed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hyder yr profits rise, savings eyed.

text.p: British multi-utility Hyder Plc turned in a strong rise in annual profits on Monday, but said further cuts in operational costs could mean job losses from its merged water and electricity businesses.
It also warned the new Labour government that extra investment and customer rebates could be hit if plans for a one-off tax on the "excess profits" of privatised utilities were too onerous.

Hyder said pre-tax profits for the year ending March 31 were within expectations at 208.2 million pounds ($339.8 million), a strong rise from 112.9 million previously. The dividend also rose sharply to 43.9 pence per share from 38.7 pence.
Shares in the company were up 5.5 pence to 824.5 pence in late morning trade after touching an early high of 827 pence.

Finance director Paul Twamley told Reuters that a study of operational activities was currently underway which could result in further cost reductions including possible job cuts, although these would be on a voluntary basis.

Hyder, which was formed when Welsh Water took over South Wales Electricity (Swalec) at the beginning of 1996, has already secured cost savings of 35.7 million pounds from the merger this year, ahead of a target 27 million.

The company said cost reduction programmes in its electricity, water and services businesses continued ahead of target. Staffing levels had been targeted to drop to 4,590 by 1999 from current levels of 5,050 under the existing merger strategy.
"Operating two utilities in the same geography continues to generate significant efficiencies and gave rise to earnings enhancement in excess of 17 percent in the year," the company said.
Twamley told Reuters that Hyder's target for cost savings from the merger had been 75 million pounds by 2000, adding that "we're halfway there".
Gearing rose to 100 percent from 95 percent in the previous period, however.

Hyder said that "In the longer term, utility efficiency benefits will become increasingly difficult to achieve and (we) have focused on ways of growing our non-regulated profits to underpin long-term dividend growth."
Profit before interest from its non-regulated activities was 32.6 million pounds in the year, or 11.5 percent of total.

Twamley said Hyder intended to increase its investment in non-regulated infrastructure projects worldwide by more than 30 million pounds a year from current levels of 70 million, but in relatively low-risk projects.
"We're looking for 15 percent post-tax real (rate of return on capital) on our portfolio," he said.
The 11 percent real dividend growth was considered sustainable, Twamley said, but he warned that the company was not forecasting dividend growth or cover levels.
Strategy would not change, he added, if a one-off tax on the "excess profits" of privatised utilities proposed by the new Labour government was at a "reasonable" level.
The government, which rolled into power with a huge majority on May 1, has vowed to introduce a so-called "windfall" tax as a central plank of its first budget, to be announced on July 2.
Twamley said the dividend growth of 11 percent was declared "knowing that there is going to be a windfall tax... we have to take that into account in what we do".
He said Hyder was not calculating a specific figure for the proposed tax but was considering a range of possibilities.
But he warned that discretionary spending, including that for the environment, along with customer rebates could be hit if the windfall levy was too high.
"Those sort of discretionary spends, discretionary rebates are the things that may become vulnerable in the event that the windfall tax was too onerous," he said.
He added Hyder had no problems with a 10-point plan proposed by the government to tackle the problems of the country's worst drought in 200 years, drawn up mid-May.
Hyder has signed up to the plan, which includes proposals for mandatory targets to cut leakage, which currently sees nearly 800 million gallons a day seep out of pipes. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
